content: Tinidazole is an antimicrobial agent with both antiprotozoal and antibacterial properties. Its mechanism of action involves the reduction of its nitro group by cellular extracts of Trichomonas. This reduction process generates free nitro radicals, which are believed to contribute to its antiprotozoal activity. Chemically reduced tinidazole has been shown to release nitrites and cause damage to purified bacterial DNA in laboratory studies. Furthermore, tinidazole induces DNA base changes in bacterial cells and DNA strand breakage in mammalian cells. However, the exact mechanism by which tinidazole acts against Giardia and Entamoeba species remains unknown. In the context of bacterial vaginosis, culture and sensitivity testing of bacteria are not routinely performed for diagnostic purposes. Standardized methods for susceptibility testing of potential bacterial pathogens such as Gardnerella vaginalis, Mobiluncus species, or Mycoplasma hominis have not been established. Available in vitro data indicate that tinidazole is active against most strains of organisms associated with bacterial vaginosis, including Bacteroides species, Gardnerella vaginalis, and Prevotella species. However, tinidazole does not appear to exhibit activity against most strains of vaginal lactobacilli. Tinidazole demonstrates both in vitro and clinical activity against the following protozoa: Trichomonas vaginalis, Giardia duodenalis (also known as G. lamblia), and Entamoeba histolytica. For protozoal parasites, standardized susceptibility tests are not available for use in clinical microbiology laboratories. The development of resistance to tinidazole by Giardia duodenalis, Entamoeba histolytica, or bacteria associated with bacterial vaginosis has not been studied. Approximately 38% of Trichomonas vaginalis isolates with reduced susceptibility to metronidazole also exhibit reduced susceptibility to tinidazole in vitro. However, the clinical significance of this cross-resistance is not yet understood.
